questions.q: Define 'imagery' in poetry and give one example from the poem "olar vk;k" without quoting the entire line.
questions.a: Imagery is the use of descriptive language that appeals to the senses (sight, sound, touch, taste, smell) to create a vivid mental picture. In "olar vk;k", the phrase "f[kyh gqbZ gok vkbZ] fiQjdh&lh vkbZ" (parched, cracked earth) is visual and tactile imagery — it lets us see the fissures and feel the heat. A wrong answer that merely says "imagery is a picture" reveals the student confuses the device with its effect; they miss the sensory dimension that makes imagery functional.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the poet repeats the word "rksM+ks" (chop/cut) three times at the start of the second poem. What happens to the tone if you read it only once?
questions.a: The triple repetition ("rksM+ks rksM+ks rksM+ks") mimics the rhythmic, relentless swing of an axe — it enacts the physical labor and also suggests an obsessive, almost ritualistic urgency. Reading it once flattens the tone into a simple command; the repetition transforms it into a chant of survival. A student who says "it emphasizes cutting" has identified the surface function but misses the performative dimension — the sound *becomes* the action.

questions.q: In "olar vk;k", the line "vkSj ;g oSQysaMj ls ekywe Fkk" (and this news came from the newspaper) appears after a stanza of vivid rural decay. Apply the concept of 'juxtaposition' to explain the effect of this sudden shift.
questions.a: Step 1: Identify the two elements juxtaposed — the slow, sensory decay of the village (stanzas 1–2) and the cold, impersonal medium of the newspaper (stanza 3). Step 2: Note the contrast in diction: "ngj&ngj", "fiQjdh" (organic, oral) vs. "oSQysaMj" (modern, printed). Step 3: Explain the effect — the newspaper reduces a lived tragedy to a distant report, highlighting the disconnect between urban media and rural reality. Step 4: Link to theme — this juxtaposition underscores the poem's critique of how mainstream discourse erases marginalized voices. A wrong answer that only says "it shows contrast" fails to trace *how* the contrast operates through diction and *why* it matters for the theme.

questions.q: Compare the use of the 'tree' image in both poems: in "olar vk;k" it is "xje ikuh" (the shade tree) and in "rksM+ks" it is "Ålj catj" (the green tree). Analyze how the same symbol carries opposite emotional valences.
questions.a: In "olar vk;k", "xje ikuh" (the shade tree) is a memory of relief — "ugkbZ gks" (it used to be) marks its absence; the tree symbolizes lost ecological and communal shelter. In "rksM+ks", "Ålj catj" is actively being felled ("rksM+ks") — the tree is a living entity whose destruction is both necessary for survival ("l`tu") and a wound ("eu dh [kht"). The first poem mourns what is *gone*; the second enacts the *act of losing*. A student who writes "both poems use trees" without distinguishing absence vs. act, nostalgia vs. necessity, has not analyzed — they have only listed.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "The poet's use of colloquial dialect (e.g., 'pqjeqjk', 'fiQjdh', 'ngj&ngj') makes the poems authentic but limits their universal appeal." Defend or refute with evidence from the text.
questions.a: Refute. The dialect words are not decorative; they carry precise ecological and cultural knowledge — "pqjeqjk" (a specific bird's call signaling rain), "fiQjdh" (earth cracked in a network pattern), "ngj&ngj" (the sound of deep fissures). These terms encode generations of agrarian observation that standard Hindi cannot capture. Their specificity *creates* universality: the reader feels the particularity of this drought, which then resonates with any marginalized community facing erasure. A student who agrees with the claim treats dialect as a barrier rather than a conduit; they miss how local texture enables global empathy.

questions.q: Write a four-line stanza in the voice of the farmer from "olar vk;k" that uses at least two sound devices (alliteration, onomatopoeia, assonance) to convey the sound of the wind over cracked fields.
questions.a: Example: "ngh&ngh xk;u chlkc] fiQjdh ds i'kq esa / jax&jl xqykc nwj] uanu ou dk vfHkO;fDr" — uses alliteration ("ngh&ngh", "chlkc", "fiQjdh") and onomatopoeia ("xk;u", "jax&jl") to mimic wind whistling through cracks. A poor answer writes a generic sad poem without sound devices, showing the student cannot transfer analytical insight into creative practice — they know *what* devices are but not *how* to deploy them for effect.
